items.meaning: I / me (two common sentence forms)
items.example: Ako si Mia. Maayo ra ko.
items.hint: Ako is the full topic or emphasized form. Ko is the short form that commonly follows the predicate.

items.meaning: you (singular; two common sentence forms)
items.hint: Ikaw is full or emphasized. Ka is the short singular form that usually follows the predicate.

items.meaning: he / she
items.natural: He or she is a teacher.
items.hint: Cebuano siya does not distinguish male and female.

items.meaning: we, including you / we, excluding you
items.natural: Let’s eat, including you. We are from Cebu, not necessarily including you.
items.hint: Kita includes the listener. Kami excludes the listener. This difference changes the meaning.

items.meaning: you all / they
items.natural: How are you all? They are well.
items.hint: Kamo addresses more than one person. Sila refers to more than one third person.

items.meaning: my / your / his or her, before a noun
items.example: Akong ngalan. Imong balay. Iyang trabaho.
items.natural: My name. Your house. His or her job.
items.hint: These forms contain a possessive pronoun plus the linker -ng.

items.meaning: marks the main or focused common noun phrase
items.hint: Ang does not simply equal English ‘the’. It marks the noun phrase being presented as the sentence topic or focus.

items.meaning: marks a personal name in the main or focused role
items.hint: Use si before one person’s name where ang would mark a common noun.

items.meaning: introduces many non-focused or indefinite nouns, including objects
items.hint: Og is common in teaching materials; ug is a widespread spelling and pronunciation alternative. The same written ug can also mean ‘and’ in context.

items.meaning: marks locations and many specific or oblique noun phrases
items.hint: Sa often corresponds to English in, at, to, from, or a specific non-focused phrase; context decides the translation.

items.meaning: plural marker for nouns
items.hint: Mga signals more than one but does not itself give an exact number.

items.meaning: links a modifier and the word it describes
items.hint: Use separate nga after many consonant-final words. After a vowel, the linker often attaches as -ng.

items.meaning: here by me / there by you / over there
items.natural: Here only. The market is over there.
items.hint: Everyday regional usage varies, but the basic three-way contrast is near the speaker, near the listener, and far from both.

items.meaning: this / that / that over there
items.natural: How much is this? I want that.
items.hint: The forms reflect distance. Shorter spoken forms such as ni, na, and to are also common in context.

items.meaning: yes-or-no question particle
items.hint: Ba explicitly marks a yes-or-no question. Intonation can also signal a question in many short phrases.

items.meaning: just / only
items.hint: Ra is strongly Cebuano. Lang is also very common and is historically shared through regional contact. Choice depends on the phrase and speaker.

items.meaning: also / too
items.hint: Pud and sad are common regional alternatives. Preserve the speaker’s natural local form.

items.meaning: still or more / now or already
items.natural: One more. There is none left now.
items.hint: Pa often keeps something continuing or adds more. Na signals a changed or current state.

items.meaning: adds explanation, contrast, or conversational emphasis
items.natural: I’m fine, actually / I am fine.
items.hint: Man rarely has one fixed English translation. Its effect depends on context and tone.

items.meaning: really / indeed / definitely
items.hint: Gyud and jud are common spelling and pronunciation variants used for strong emphasis.

dialogue.title: Crossing Grammar Bridge
dialogue.note: The dialogue recycles familiar language while highlighting short pronouns, markers, the linker, location words, and particles. The goal is recognition and controlled use, not memorising abstract labels.

lines.speaker: A
lines.natural: This is Ana. She is a teacher.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Taga-Bohol siya, pero nagpuyo siya sa Cebu.
lines.literal: From-Bohol she, but lives she [LOC] Cebu.
lines.natural: She is from Bohol, but she lives in Cebu.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Maayo ra ba siya mosulti og Binisaya?
lines.literal: Well just Q she speak [OBJ] Bisaya?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Oo, maayo gyud. Nakat-on pud siya og English.
lines.literal: Yes, well indeed. Learned also she [OBJ] English.
lines.natural: Yes, very well. She is also learning English.

starterExercises.prompt: Which pronoun means ‘we, including the listener’?
Which marker is used before one person’s name?
What is the difference between kita and kami?
starterExercises.answer: Kita includes the listener; kami excludes the listener.
choices: Kita includes the listener; kami excludes the listener.
Kita is singular; kami is plural.
Kita means they; kami means you all.
